title: Valsalva Retinopathy: Understanding Acute Pre-Retinal Hemorrhage
summary: Valsalva Retinopathy (VR) is a condition characterized by acute pre-retinal hemorrhage, typically in the macula, triggered by a sudden increase in intrathoracic or intra-abdominal pressure. While often self-limiting, it causes abrupt vision loss and necessitates careful differential diagnosis to rule out more serious underlying pathologies. Management primarily involves observation, with laser or surgical intervention for persistent cases.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Valsalva Retinopathy (VR) is an acute, typically unilateral, pre-retinal hemorrhage occurring as a consequence of a sudden, transient elevation in intrathoracic and/or intra-abdominal pressure. This pressure surge transmits to the choroidal and retinal venous systems, leading to a rupture of superficial retinal capillaries, most commonly in the macular region. It typically presents as sudden, painless vision loss.

sections.title: 2. Epidemiology & Risk Factors
content: **Incidence:** Relatively uncommon, but often under-diagnosed due to spontaneous resolution.
**Demographics:** Predominantly affects young to middle-aged adults (20-40 years old) with no underlying systemic comorbidities, but can occur at any age.
**Sex:** No significant sex predilection.
**Risk Factors (Valsalva Maneuvers):**
• Intense physical exertion (e.g., weightlifting, vigorous exercise)
• Straining (e.g., defecation, coughing, vomiting, sneezing)
• Childbirth/Labor
• Blowing musical instruments (e.g., trumpet, saxophone)
• Scuba diving, flying
• Choking or strangulation
• Emesis (especially hyperemesis gravidarum)

sections.title: 3. Etiology & Pathophysiology
content: **Step 1: Valsalva Maneuver Initiation** – Patient performs an action that significantly increases intrathoracic or intra-abdominal pressure (e.g., forced expiration against a closed glottis).
**Step 2: Venous Pressure Surge** – This pressure is transmitted to the superior vena cava and jugular veins, leading to a rapid and substantial rise in episcleral and intraocular venous pressure.
**Step 3: Retinal Capillary Stress** – The sudden elevation in retinal venous pressure, particularly in the perifoveal capillaries, overwhelms their structural integrity.
**Step 4: Capillary Rupture** – Fragile superficial retinal capillaries rupture due to the increased transmural pressure.

**Step 5: Hemorrhage Formation** – Blood extravasates into the potential spaces in front of the retina, most commonly in the sub-internal limiting membrane (sub-ILM) or sub-hyaloid space, forming a localized pre-retinal hemorrhage.

sections.title: 4. Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: **Acute Onset:** Symptoms appear suddenly, often immediately after the Valsalva event.
**Painless Vision Loss:** The hallmark symptom, ranging from mild blurring to severe decrease in central visual acuity, depending on hemorrhage size and location.
**Floaters:** Patients often report numerous black or red 'floaters' corresponding to the blood cells in the vitreous or blood behind the ILM/hyaloid.
**Central Scotoma:** A blind spot in the central visual field.
**Metamorphopsia:** Less common, but can occur if there is underlying retinal distortion.
**Unilateral:** Typically affects one eye, though bilateral cases have been reported rarely.

sections.title: 5. Ocular Examination Findings
content: **Visual Acuity (VA):** Variable, from 20/20 to hand motion, depending on the density and location of the hemorrhage (macular involvement causes significant drop).
**Anterior Segment:** Usually quiet, no signs of inflammation or hemorrhage.
**Pupils:** Normal, reactive.
**Fundoscopy (Dilated):**
• Well-demarcated, usually round or oval, bright red hemorrhage located anterior to the retina.
• Commonly observed in the macula or posterior pole.
• May appear 'boat-shaped' or 'dumbbell-shaped' if the hemorrhage is sub-hyaloid with fluid levels due to gravity.
• Retinal vessels appear normal, no signs of vasculitis or occlusion.
**Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT):**

• Crucial for identifying the exact location of hemorrhage: either between the retina and the internal limiting membrane (sub-ILM hemorrhage) or between the ILM and the posterior hyaloid face (sub-hyaloid hemorrhage).
• Demonstrates an optically empty or moderately reflective space anterior to the retina, containing hyper-reflective material (blood).
• The ILM and hyaloid membrane can often be clearly visualized.

sections.title: 6. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **Step 1: Comprehensive Ophthalmic Examination**
• Best-corrected visual acuity, slit-lamp biomicroscopy, dilated fundus examination.
**Step 2: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) of the Macula**
• Essential for localizing the hemorrhage (sub-ILM vs. sub-hyaloid) and assessing underlying retinal structures. Also helps exclude choroidal neovascularization or other macular pathologies.
**Step 3: Fundus Photography**
• Documents the size, shape, and location of the hemorrhage for baseline and follow-up.
**Step 4: Fluorescein Angiography (FFA) (If indicated)**
• Typically not required for classic VR, as retinal circulation is usually normal.

• May be performed to rule out other causes of hemorrhage (e.g., retinal macroaneurysm, CNVM, retinal vasculitis) if the diagnosis is uncertain. Usually shows blockage of choroidal and retinal fluorescence.
**Step 5: B-scan Ultrasonography (If view obscured)**
• If the hemorrhage is very dense or there's an associated vitreous hemorrhage obscuring fundus view, B-scan can evaluate for retinal detachment or other posterior segment pathologies.
**Step 6: Systemic Workup (If suspicion of underlying systemic cause)**
• Complete Blood Count (CBC) with platelet count (to rule out anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukemia).
• Coagulation Profile (PT/INR, aPTT) (if bleeding disorder or anticoagulant use suspected).
• Blood Pressure measurement (to rule out hypertensive retinopathy).

sections.title: 7. Differential Diagnosis of Acute Macular Hemorrhage

rows: Retinal Vein Occlusion (RVO)
No tortuosity/dilatation of retinal veins. No cotton wool spots, usually localized single hemorrhage.
Widespread retinal hemorrhages, tortuous and dilated veins, cotton wool spots, disc edema, often sectoral distribution (BRVO) or diffuse (CRVO).
Diabetic Retinopathy (DR)
Absence of other DR signs (microaneurysms, exudates, neovascularization).
Microaneurysms, hard exudates, cotton wool spots, intraretinal hemorrhages, neovascularization (PDR), macular edema.
Hypertensive Retinopathy
Normal blood pressure, no other signs of hypertensive damage.
Arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, cotton wool spots, flame-shaped hemorrhages, optic disc edema in severe cases.
Retinal Arterial Macroaneurysm (RAM) Rupture
No saccular arterial dilatation. Hemorrhage usually single and localized to the macroaneurysm.
Saccular dilatation on an arteriole, often with surrounding lipid exudates, intraretinal/subretinal/vitreous hemorrhage. FFA confirms leakage.
Wet Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD)
No drusen, RPE changes, or underlying choroidal neovascularization (CNV).
Drusen, RPE atrophy/hyperplasia, subretinal fluid, subretinal hemorrhage, CNV complex visible on OCT/FFA.
Terson's Syndrome
No history of acute intracranial event (e.g., subarachnoid hemorrhage).
History of subarachnoid hemorrhage or other intracranial bleed, often bilateral intraocular hemorrhages (vitreous, sub-hyaloid, sub-ILM, intraretinal).
Traumatic Retinopathy (Purtscher's-like)
No history of significant ocular or systemic trauma.
Multiple cotton wool spots, retinal hemorrhages (often multi-layered), arterial narrowing after trauma or severe systemic insult (e.g., pancreatitis, fat embolism).
Pathological Myopia with CNVM
No high myopia, lacquer cracks, or CNV features on OCT/FFA.
High myopia, lacquer cracks, Fuchs spot, development of CNV, subretinal hemorrhage/fluid.
Anemic/Thrombocytopenic Retinopathy
Normal CBC and platelet count.
Roth spots (hemorrhages with white centers), scattered intraretinal hemorrhages, often bilateral. Systemic signs of anemia/thrombocytopenia.
Leukemia/Lymphoma Retinopathy
No systemic signs of hematological malignancy.
White-centered hemorrhages (Roth spots), venous tortuosity, cotton wool spots, infiltrates. Systemic diagnosis of leukemia/lymphoma.
Pre-eclampsia/Eclampsia
No history of pregnancy-related hypertension.
Retinal edema, exudates, serous retinal detachment, hemorrhages in pregnant patients with severe hypertension and proteinuria.

sections.title: 8. Management & Treatment Protocol
content: **Step 1: Observation (First Line)**
• The vast majority (80-90%) of Valsalva hemorrhages resolve spontaneously within 2-6 months, with good visual recovery.
• Hemoglobin breakdown products are absorbed, and the blood disperses or drains. Regular follow-up every 2-4 weeks is advised to monitor resolution and visual acuity.
**Step 2: Patient Education & Counseling**
• Explain the benign nature and favorable prognosis. Advise avoiding activities that induce Valsalva maneuvers (e.g., straining, heavy lifting) temporarily.
**Step 3: Nd:YAG Laser Membranotomy (Consider after 2-4 weeks if non-resolving)**
• **Indication:** Dense, non-resolving sub-hyaloid or sub-ILM hemorrhage significantly affecting central vision, typically after 2-4 weeks of observation.
• **Technique:** A small opening is created in the anterior limiting membrane (ILM or posterior hyaloid) to allow the blood to drain into the vitreous cavity, where it disperses more quickly.

• **Parameters:** Typically 1-3 mJ, 1-3 pulses per shot, targeting the superior-most edge of the hemorrhage (to allow gravity-assisted drainage and avoid direct foveal trauma). Use a contact lens (e.g., Abraham lens).

• **Risks:** Macular hole formation, retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) damage, iatrogenic retinal hemorrhage, vitreous hemorrhage (from drainage), epiretinal membrane (ERM) formation, increased intraocular pressure (IOP).
**Step 4: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) (Reserved for specific cases)**
• **Indications:**
• Very dense, non-resolving hemorrhage (especially vitreous hemorrhage) that fails to clear after extended observation or Nd:YAG laser.
• Associated complications like epiretinal membrane (ERM) or macular hole.
• Co-existing retinal detachment or other pathologies requiring surgical intervention.
• Chronic, organized sub-ILM hemorrhage that could induce ERM or traction.
• **Technique:** Standard 3-port vitrectomy to remove vitreous and hemorrhage, potentially peeling the ILM if necessary to prevent ERM. Gas or oil tamponade may be used.

sections.title: 9. Complications & Prognosis
content: **Complications (Rare):**
• **Macular hole:** Can occur spontaneously during resolution or as a complication of Nd:YAG laser.
• **Epiretinal Membrane (ERM):** May form secondary to inflammation or fibrous organization, leading to persistent metamorphopsia or vision loss.
• **Vitreous Hemorrhage:** If the hemorrhage breaks through the posterior hyaloid into the vitreous, causing significant vision loss and potentially requiring vitrectomy.
• **Iron-induced toxicity:** Rarely, hemosiderosis can cause retinal toxicity if hemorrhage persists for a very long time.
• **Persistent Scotoma/Vision Loss:** If damage to photoreceptors or RPE occurs, or if ERM/macular hole develops.
**Prognosis:**
• Generally excellent. Most patients achieve complete or near-complete visual recovery to baseline, especially with spontaneous resolution.
• Even with Nd:YAG laser, visual outcomes are typically good, with faster recovery compared to observation alone.

sections.title: 10. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: **Sudden vision loss accompanied by severe headache, nausea/vomiting, neck stiffness, or altered mental status:** Suggests possible intracranial hemorrhage (e.g., subarachnoid hemorrhage) with associated Terson's syndrome.
**Signs of systemic bleeding disorders:** Easy bruising, prolonged bleeding, or petechiae, necessitating urgent hematological evaluation.
**Rapidly worsening vision in both eyes:** Indicates a more widespread or severe systemic condition.
**Non-resolving dense hemorrhage with evidence of retinal toxicity (e.g., changes in RPE or photoreceptors on OCT):** May warrant earlier intervention.
**Associated retinal detachment or other acute intraocular pathology.**

sections.title: 12. Key Clinical Pearls
content: Valsalva Retinopathy typically affects young, otherwise healthy individuals.
A detailed history of recent strenuous activity is crucial for diagnosis.
OCT is indispensable for confirming the pre-retinal location (sub-ILM or sub-hyaloid) and ruling out other macular pathologies.
Most cases are self-limiting and resolve with excellent visual recovery without intervention.
Nd:YAG laser membranotomy can accelerate visual recovery in selected cases but carries risks.
Always consider and rule out Terson's syndrome if there's any suspicion of intracranial pathology.
A systemic workup is warranted if there are any atypical features or suspicion of underlying bleeding disorders.

sections.title: 13. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: While the fundamental understanding and management of Valsalva Retinopathy remain consistent, recent advances primarily lie in improved diagnostic imaging. High-resolution OCT has revolutionized the ability to precisely identify the layer of hemorrhage (sub-ILM vs. sub-hyaloid), which can influence the timing and approach to Nd:YAG laser treatment. Studies often focus on comparing visual outcomes and complication rates between observation, Nd:YAG laser, and vitrectomy, consistently affirming the generally favorable prognosis across management strategies. There are no recent landmark studies that have drastically altered the treatment paradigm, but continuous refinement of laser parameters and vitrectomy techniques for complications is ongoing.

sections.title: 14. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: **Children:** While less common, VR can occur in children due to severe coughing (e.g., pertussis), vomiting, or strenuous play. In infants, retinal hemorrhages, particularly multi-layered and bilateral, must raise suspicion for **Non-Accidental Trauma (Shaken Baby Syndrome)**.

**Pregnant Women:** Valsalva retinopathy can occur during labor. It is important to differentiate it from other causes of retinal hemorrhage in pregnancy, such as pre-eclampsia/eclampsia-related retinopathy, which has distinct features (e.g., serous detachments, exudates, severe hypertension).

**Elderly:** Although less frequent in this group, elderly patients may be on anticoagulant or antiplatelet medications, which can exacerbate the extent or duration of the hemorrhage. Careful medication history and systemic workup are crucial.
